newsitem.title: UK: WORLD BONDS - Buy U.S. over Europe for long haul.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS - Buy U.S. over Europe for long haul.

text.p: Speculation of further interest rates rises will continue to dog Treasuries short-term but the U.S. will clearly outperform Europe by the end of the year as the economic prospects of each region reverse, analysts said on Wednesday.
The only question, they said, is when to jump into the U.S. market. And that depends on the chances and timing of another rate rise.

"If we do get two more tightenings out of the way in the U.S., people will start to look into 1998 and expect German rates to start rising and U.S. rates to even flatten," David Hewitt, bond strategist at Tokyo-Mitsubishi International in London, said.
By 1043 GMT, the 10-year T-note/Bund yield gap was at 111 basis points, near the top of the range of 115 since the end of February.

Analysts said that gap would likely widen next week as the U.S. market negotiated a week laced with heavy-weight data, including the employment cost index, consumer confidence and the March employment report.

All the data would be thoroughly combed to determine whether the Federal Reserve would raise rates again at its May 20 meeting. The central bank raised its Fed funds target rate by 25 basis points to 5.50 percent on March 25 and Treasuries have been anticipating the next move ever since.
Hewitt expected another two to three rate rises to bring the target rate to 6.00 or 6.25 percent, sending the T-note/Bund gap to around 135 basis points.
But into the second half of the year the U.S. economy should begin to settle down, just as the German economy begins to lift off, squeezing the gap to around 75 basis points by the end of the year.
In the meantime, Hewitt said he was advising investors to buy the two-to-five-year area of the Treasury curve, which has already priced in a lot of rate tightening.

Helen Morrissey, director of fixed income at Newton Investment Management in London, with 1.0 billion stg in fixed income, said Newton began buying Treasuries when the yield on the long bond reached a recent high of around 7.17 percent.
"We have been buying some but what we have not done is spent every bean," she said, adding further buying opportunities could arise as the fed fund rate goes up another 50 basis points.

"Over a more medium term, I see troubles ahead for Germany whichever way you look at it. If they have a bit of economic growth people start worrying about interest rate tightening, even if it is premature. If they have no growth the fiscal situation is difficult," she said.

"In the longer term the U.S. is good value, once the market realises wage inflation is offset by some deflationary forces," she added, citing low commodity prices, a stronger dollar and global competition.
Stephen Lewis, chief economist at London Bond Broking here, would sell Bunds to buy Treasuries now. He does not expect the Fed to raise rates in May.

"It wants to underline the differences between the present policy and the one pursued in 1994 when rate rises came thick and fast," he said. He added recent comments from Federal Reserve vice chairwoman Alice Rivlin stressed the last rate rise was an insurance policy.
"Fed officials used that last year about the move down from 5.50 to 5.25 percent...and there was only one move," he said.

Lewis would buy the long end, forecasting the 30-year yield to drop to 6.50 percent by the end of the year from 7.05 percent now and the T-note/Bund gap to squeeze to around 55 basis points the end of 1997. --Jacqueline Thorpe, International Bonds Unit +44 171 542 6176
